prompt: Why are epoxides cleaved by acid under much milder conditions than other ethers?

choices.text: Their oxygen carries a full positive charge
choices.why: An epoxide oxygen is neutral until it is protonated. The ease of cleavage comes from ring strain.

choices.text: They contain a carbon–oxygen double bond
choices.why: Epoxides have only single bonds; they are cyclic ethers.

choices.text: They are opened by an E1 elimination that other ethers can't undergo
choices.why: Acid-catalyzed opening is S_N2-like backside attack by a nucleophile, not an elimination.

explanation: Epoxides are cleaved by acid just as other ethers are, but under much milder conditions because of ring strain. Dilute aqueous acid at room temperature is enough to hydrolyze an epoxide to a 1,2-diol, whereas ordinary ethers need strong acids such as HBr or HI.

prompt: Acid hydrolysis of an epoxide gives a 1,2-diol, also called a vicinal glycol. What does vicinal mean?

choices.text: Adjacent: the two –OH groups are on neighboring carbons
Same: both –OH groups are on one carbon
choices.why: Vicinal means adjacent. In a 1,2-diol the two –OH groups are on neighboring carbons, not on the same one.

choices.text: Opposite: the –OH groups are at the two ends of the chain
choices.why: Vicinal means adjacent, as the 1,2 numbering shows.

choices.text: Cyclic: the two –OH groups are part of a ring
choices.why: Vicinal refers to neighboring positions, not to a ring.

explanation: The word vicinal means "adjacent," and a glycol is a diol. A vicinal glycol is therefore a 1,2-diol, with –OH groups on neighboring carbons.

prompt: What product forms when 1,2-epoxycyclohexane is treated with dilute aqueous acid at room temperature?

choices.why: Water attacks the protonated epoxide from the back side, so the two –OH groups end up trans.
Ring-opening leaves an –OH group on each of the two former epoxide carbons.
Acid opens the ring by nucleophilic attack; it doesn't remove the oxygen.

explanation: Epoxide cleavage takes place by S_N2-like backside attack of a nucleophile on the protonated epoxide, giving a trans-1,2-diol. 1,2-Epoxycyclohexane gives trans-1,2-cyclohexanediol (86%).

prompt: 1,2-Epoxycyclohexane is treated with anhydrous HBr in ether. What is the product?

choices.why: Bromide attacks the protonated epoxide from the back side, so –Br and –OH end up trans.
A diol needs water as the nucleophile. With anhydrous HX, the halide ion opens the ring.
Ring-opening keeps the oxygen as an –OH group on the neighboring carbon.

explanation: Epoxides can be opened by acids other than H3O+. With anhydrous HX, the halide ion attacks the protonated epoxide from the back side, converting the epoxide into a trans halohydrin.

prompt: What is the major product when 1,2-epoxypropane reacts with HCl?

choices.why: That needs attack at the secondary carbon. When both epoxide carbons are primary or secondary, chloride attacks the less substituted one.
A diol forms with water. With HCl, chloride ion opens the ring.
One HCl opens the ring, putting Cl on one carbon and leaving –OH on the other.

explanation: When both epoxide carbons are primary or secondary, nucleophilic attack occurs primarily at the less highly substituted site, an S_N2-like result. 1,2-Epoxypropane and HCl therefore give primarily 1-chloro-2-propanol.

prompt: What is the major product when 2-methyl-1,2-epoxypropane reacts with HCl?

choices.why: Attack at the less substituted carbon is the rule only when both carbons are primary or secondary. Here one carbon is tertiary.
A diol would form with water. HCl supplies chloride ion as the nucleophile.
Ring-opening keeps the oxygen, which becomes an –OH group on the other carbon.

explanation: When one of the epoxide carbons is tertiary, nucleophilic attack occurs primarily at the more highly substituted site, an S_N1-like result. Chloride bonds to the tertiary carbon, giving 2-chloro-2-methyl-1-propanol as the major product.

prompt: 1,2-Epoxy-1-methylcyclohexane, in which a methyl group is on one of the epoxide carbons, reacts with HBr. What is the product?

choices.why: Bromide attacks from the back side of the protonated epoxide, so a single stereoisomer forms with –Br and –OH trans.
That puts Br on the secondary carbon. With a tertiary epoxide carbon, Br− attacks the more substituted site.

choices.text: A mixture of cis- and trans-2-bromo-2-methylcyclohexanol
choices.why: Only a single stereoisomer forms, the one with –Br and –OH trans.

explanation: The reaction yields only a single stereoisomer of 2-bromo-2-methylcyclohexanol, in which the –Br and –OH groups are trans (Figure 18.5.1). Backside attack gives the trans product, an S_N2-like result, while attack at the tertiary carbon is an S_N1-like result.

prompt: In the reaction of 1,2-epoxy-1-methylcyclohexane with HBr, which observation is an S_N1-like result?

choices.text: Br− attacks the more hindered tertiary carbon
The –Br and –OH groups end up trans
choices.why: Trans groups result from backside displacement of the epoxide oxygen, an S_N2-like result.
A single stereoisomer means attack from one side only, an S_N2-like feature.

choices.text: The nucleophile attacks from the side opposite the oxygen
choices.why: Backside attack is the S_N2-like feature of the reaction.

explanation: Acid-catalyzed epoxide openings are midway between S_N1 and S_N2. The transition state has S_N2-like geometry, so attack is from the back side and gives a trans product. But it also has a high degree of S_N1-like carbocation character: the positive charge is shared by the more highly substituted carbon, so Br− attacks the tertiary carbon.

prompt: Cyclohexyloxirane is an epoxide in which one ring carbon carries a cyclohexyl group (C6H11) and an H, and the other is a CH2. What is the major product when it reacts with HCl in ether?

choices.why: That needs attack at the secondary carbon. With only primary and secondary epoxide carbons, chloride attacks the primary carbon.
A diol forms with water. With HCl, chloride ion opens the ring.
Ring-opening keeps the oxygen as an –OH group on the other epoxide carbon.

explanation: One epoxide carbon is secondary and the other is primary. An epoxide with only primary and secondary carbons usually undergoes S_N2-like attack at the less hindered carbon, so chloride attacks the CH2, giving 2-chloro-1-cyclohexylethanol (Worked Example 18.5.1).

prompt: In 3-cyclohexyl-2,2-dimethyloxirane, one epoxide carbon carries two methyl groups and the other carries a cyclohexyl group (C6H11) and an H. What is the major product with HCl in ether?

choices.why: That is attack at the secondary carbon. When one epoxide carbon is tertiary, the nucleophile attacks the more substituted site.
Water would give a diol. Here chloride ion is the nucleophile.
Ring-opening puts Cl and OH on the two different former epoxide carbons, not both on one.

explanation: One epoxide carbon is tertiary (it carries two methyl groups), so under acidic conditions attack occurs primarily at that more substituted carbon, an S_N1-like result. Chloride ends up on the tertiary carbon and –OH on the carbon bearing the cyclohexyl group (Exercise 18.5.1a).

prompt: Methylenecyclohexane oxide has an epoxide ring made of one cyclohexane ring carbon, a CH2 group, and oxygen. What is the major product when it reacts with HCl in ether?

choices.text: A cyclohexane carbon bearing both –Cl and a –CH2OH group
A cyclohexane carbon bearing both –OH and a –CH2Cl group
choices.why: That comes from attack at the CH2 carbon. The ring carbon is tertiary, so under acidic conditions chloride attacks there.

choices.text: A cyclohexane carbon bearing both –OH and a –CH2OH group
choices.why: That diol forms with water or hydroxide. With HCl, chloride is the nucleophile.

choices.text: A cyclohexane carbon bearing both –Cl and a –CH2Cl group
choices.why: One HCl opens the ring, and the other epoxide carbon keeps the oxygen as an –OH group.

explanation: The epoxide carbon that belongs to the cyclohexane ring is tertiary, so in acid, chloride attacks it, an S_N1-like result. The product is (1-chlorocyclohexyl)methanol, with Cl on the ring carbon and a –CH2OH group beside it (Exercise 18.5.1b).

prompt: 2-Ethyl-2-methyloxirane has one epoxide carbon bearing an ethyl and a methyl group and another that is a CH2. It is opened by ^18O-labeled hydroxide ion, ^18OH−, in H2^18O. Where does the ^18O label end up in the diol?

choices.text: In the –OH on the primary (CH2) carbon
In the –OH on the tertiary carbon
choices.why: Base-catalyzed opening is S_N2, so hydroxide attacks the less hindered CH2 carbon.
Only one oxygen comes from the nucleophile; the other was the epoxide oxygen.

choices.text: Nowhere; the label is lost as water
choices.why: The labeled hydroxide bonds to carbon and stays in the product as an –OH group.

explanation: Base-catalyzed epoxide opening is a typical S_N2 reaction, with attack at the less hindered epoxide carbon. The ^18OH− bonds to the primary CH2, and the original epoxide oxygen stays on the tertiary carbon (Exercise 18.5.3a).

prompt: 2-Ethyl-2-methyloxirane has one epoxide carbon bearing an ethyl and a methyl group and another that is a CH2. It is opened by dilute acid in ^18O-labeled water, H2^18O. Where does the ^18O label end up in the major diol product?

choices.text: In the –OH on the tertiary carbon
In the –OH on the primary (CH2) carbon
choices.why: That's the result under basic conditions. In acid, with a tertiary epoxide carbon, water attacks the more substituted site.
Only one oxygen comes from the water; the other was the epoxide oxygen.

choices.text: Nowhere; the label is lost as water
choices.why: The labeled water bonds to carbon and stays in the product as an –OH group.

explanation: In acid-catalyzed opening, when one epoxide carbon is tertiary, nucleophilic attack occurs primarily at that more substituted carbon (an S_N1-like result). H2^18O bonds to the tertiary carbon, and the original epoxide oxygen stays on the CH2 (Exercise 18.5.3b).

prompt: How would you prepare trans-1-methyl-1,2-cyclohexanediol from 1-methylcyclohexene?

choices.text: Treat with m-chloroperoxybenzoic acid, then with H3O+
Treat with OsO4, then with NaHSO3
choices.why: OsO4 adds both oxygens from the same side, giving the cis diol (Exercise 18.5.2a).
Acid alone hydrates the alkene to an alcohol with one –OH group, not a diol.
That stops at the epoxide. Acid hydrolysis is needed to open it to the diol.

explanation: Epoxidation followed by acid-catalyzed ring-opening gives a trans-1,2-diol, because water attacks the protonated epoxide from the back side (Exercise 18.5.2b). OsO4 followed by NaHSO3 gives the cis diol instead.

prompt: How do epoxides differ from other ethers in their reactions with bases?

choices.text: Epoxides are opened by hydroxide ion at elevated temperatures; other ethers are not
Epoxides, like other ethers, are cleaved only by strong acids
choices.why: Unlike other ethers, epoxide rings can be cleaved by bases and nucleophiles as well as by acid.

choices.text: Other ethers are opened by hydroxide ion, but epoxides are not
choices.why: That's reversed. Ring strain lets epoxides react with hydroxide; ordinary ethers aren't affected by bases.

choices.text: Both are opened easily by hydroxide ion at room temperature
choices.why: Ordinary ethers aren't affected by bases, and epoxides react with hydroxide at elevated temperatures.

explanation: An ether oxygen is normally a poor leaving group in an S_N2 reaction, but the strain of the three-membered ring lets epoxides react with hydroxide ion at elevated temperatures. Other ethers are unaffected by bases.

prompt: What is the product when 1,2-epoxypropane reacts with ethoxide ion in ethanol?

choices.why: That needs attack at the secondary carbon. Base-catalyzed opening is S_N2 at the less hindered, primary carbon.
Ethoxide, not hydroxide, is the nucleophile, so an ethoxy group is added.
Ring-opening leaves the epoxide oxygen as an –OH group on the secondary carbon.

explanation: Base-catalyzed epoxide opening is a typical S_N2 reaction, with attack at the less hindered epoxide carbon. 1,2-Epoxypropane reacts with ethoxide exclusively at the primary carbon to give 1-ethoxy-2-propanol (83%).

prompt: Methylenecyclohexane oxide has an epoxide ring made of one cyclohexane ring carbon, a CH2 group, and oxygen. When it is heated with hydroxide ion, which carbon does hydroxide attack?

choices.text: The CH2 carbon, the less hindered site
The ring carbon, because it would form the more stable carbocation
choices.why: Carbocation-like attack at the more substituted carbon belongs to acid-catalyzed opening. In base, attack is S_N2 at the less hindered carbon.

choices.text: Neither carbon; hydroxide first protonates the oxygen
choices.why: Hydroxide is a base, not an acid, so it doesn't protonate the oxygen. It attacks a carbon directly.

choices.text: Both carbons equally, giving a 1 : 1 mixture
choices.why: Base-catalyzed opening is selective for the less hindered carbon.

explanation: Base-catalyzed epoxide opening is an S_N2 reaction at the less hindered epoxide carbon. Hydroxide attacks the CH2 group, and protonation of the resulting alkoxide gives 1-hydroxymethylcyclohexanol (70%).

prompt: The Grignard reagent made from 1-bromopentane reacts with ethylene oxide, and the product is treated with H3O+. How many carbon atoms does the resulting primary alcohol contain?
explanation: Ethylene oxide converts a Grignard reagent into a primary alcohol having two more carbons than the starting alkyl halide. 1-Bromopentane has five carbons, so the product, 1-heptanol, has 5 + 2 = 7.

prompt: Butylmagnesium bromide reacts with ethylene oxide in ether, and the product is treated with H3O+. What alcohol forms?

choices.why: Ethylene oxide adds two carbons, not one: 4 + 2 = 6.
The butyl group bonds to one CH2 of the epoxide, and the oxygen ends up on the other CH2, so the alcohol is primary.
The butyl group bonds to an epoxide carbon, so the chain grows by two carbons.

explanation: A Grignard reagent opens an epoxide by nucleophilic attack on a ring carbon. With ethylene oxide, protonation gives a primary alcohol having two more carbons than the starting alkyl halide: 1-bromobutane is converted into 1-hexanol (62%).

prompt: In the commercial synthesis of metoprolol, a β-blocker, what kind of nucleophile opens an epoxide ring?

choices.why: Grignard reagents can also open epoxides, but the metoprolol synthesis uses an amine.
Hydroxide would give a diol. The metoprolol synthesis uses an amine as the nucleophile.
The metoprolol example is a nucleophilic ring-opening by an amine, not an acid-catalyzed opening by HBr.

explanation: Many different nucleophiles can open epoxides, including amines (RNH2 or R2NH) and Grignard reagents (RMgX). In the commercial synthesis of metoprolol, used to treat cardiac arrhythmias, hypertension, and heart attacks, an amine opens the epoxide ring.
